It's my first time leading a team, and I'm determined to make it a successful experience.

I'm looking for participants with knowledge or skills in:

EE (Electrical Engineering)

AE (Aerospace Engineering)

CS (Computer Science)

SE (Software Engineering)

Or any other field you believe could contribute to our project! 

  I truly believe this team can do great things, regardless of the final rank we achieve. What matters most is learning, working together, and giving it our best.
summary:
We developed TITANS-63 Adventure, a first-person educational game that puts young players in the role of astronauts preparing to land on the Moon. Built in Godot, the game features an interactive spacecraft bridge and LUNA, a voiced robot guide who helps players respond to landing-system malfunctions, radar failures, and hazardous terrain. Players carry out practical tasks, operate spacecraft controls, and manage fuel, power, and time. Their decisions lead to four possible endings, with a secret ending unlocking an explorable Moon base.

Our project addresses the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning astronaut training concepts into hands-on learning. NASA lunar elevation data, surface imagery, and Apollo 14 historical references connect the experience to real exploration.

The project gives young learners a safe, engaging environment to practice problem-solving, resource planning, and safety-conscious decision-making while encouraging curiosity about space, science, and engineering.
details:
TITANS-63 Adventure is a first-person educational game that allows young players to experience the responsibilities of an astronaut preparing for a lunar landing. It combines exploration, guided problem-solving, and resource management to address the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

Players begin inside an interactive spacecraft bridge, where LUNA, a scripted robot guide, communicates through the ship’s screens using spoken instructions and subtitles. Three scenarios introduce a landing-system warning, a radar failure, and rocks obstructing the landing area. Players choose a response and then physically carry it out for example, walking to the sensor console and activating the backup height sensor. Decisions affect fuel, power, and remaining mission time. Four endings reflect the results, while safe and efficient decisions can unlock a secret ending and an explorable Moon base.

The game provides an engaging setting for practicing critical thinking, resource planning, and safety-conscious decision-making. Players can explore how a solution may save time while consuming more power, or how protecting the crew may require cancelling a landing. Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space and STEM while helping learners understand that successful missions depend on communication, reliable information, and thoughtful choices.

We developed the project using Godot Engine 4 and GDScript for movement, interactions, mission logic, interfaces, and cutscenes. Python, with libraries including NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow, supported terrain processing and audio generation. CMU Flite generated LUNA’s synthetic narration, and FFmpeg supported audio conversion. The project combines imported GLB models, image textures, and bundled WAV and Ogg audio. It is designed for a computer with keyboard and mouse controls and runs offline without API keys or specialized equipment.

NASA’s LRO/LROC Apollo 14 elevation data and matching surface imagery provide measured terrain and visual detail for the landing environment. NASA’s Apollo 14 historical references informed the malfunction and radar scenarios. Resource penalties, branching outcomes, individual rocks, and the Moon base are authored gameplay elements.

The project’s creativity comes from connecting choices to actions inside the environment. Selecting a backup sensor becomes a task the player performs, with LUNA providing directions and a visible marker identifying the control. Animated screen guidance, Moon-style movement, distinct footsteps, relaxing music, and ending cutscenes support the experience.

Our team considered scientific grounding, clear instructions, player engagement, performance, and learning through consequences. Subtitles, replayable guidance, and separate audio controls give players several ways to follow the mission. We also balanced terrain detail with runtime performance and preserved opportunities to restart and explore different decisions.
